The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 113, verses 1–5:

In this surah, Allah describes the attributes through which refuge is sought from the evil that is mentioned in this surah.

"Qul a'udhu ... al-falaq" (113:1): "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak." Among the meanings of falaq is daybreak, and another meaning is "creation," in the sense that everything from which existence and life burst forth, as stated in Surah al-An'am (95):

"Inna Allaha faliq al-habbi wa'l-nawa... yukhriju al-hayya min al-mayyit wa mukhriju al-mayyit min al-hayy" (6:95): "Indeed, Allah is the cleaver of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and is the bringer out of the dead from the living." And in the following verse (6:96):

"Faliq al-isbah ... husbanan" (6:96): "He is the cleaver of the dawn; He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning."

If falaq is taken to mean daybreak, the meaning is: the Lord of the dawn, who by spreading light protects everything from the evil that is hidden in darkness. And if falaq is taken to mean creation, the meaning is: I seek refuge in the Lord of creation, who grants protection from the evil of His creatures. Thus in both cases the meaning harmonises with the following phrase.

"Min sharri ma khalaq" (113:2): "From the evil of what He has created", that is, from the evil of all creation, absolutely and in general. Some of Allah's creatures, when they come into contact with others, sometimes produce harm through that contact, while in other circumstances the joining and contact of creatures produces good and benefit. Therefore it is taught to seek refuge from the evil of creatures so that only good remains. And Allah, who is the Creator of these creatures, is able to guide them to a path and to make arrangements such that good emerges from them and evil does not appear.

"Wa min sharri ghasiqin idha waqab" (113:3): "And from the evil of the darkness when it overspreads." Ghasiq literally means one who pours forth, and waqab refers to the opening in a mountain from which water flows. Here ghasiq means night, that is, the night and what is found in it, the night when it bursts forth and spreads over the earth. This night is itself frightening, and its fearfulness increases when in it every hidden and unknown danger may arise: for example, a savage beast may attack, a thief may enter, a deceitful enemy may show his hand, a poisonous insect or snake may bite. Then at night thoughts and whisperings attack a person; pains and sorrows are remembered; the pressure of feelings, passions and inclinations is at its height, all satanic forces are unleashed, evil signs come from every direction, and human desire is at its peak at night. In short, every apparent and hidden calamity attacks at night, because darkness has then spread over everything.

"Wa min sharri al-naffathati fi al-uqad" (113:4): "And from the evil of those who blow on knots." Who are those who blow on knots? They are the sorceresses who afflict people by casting spells on the senses, who deceive the nerves, give suggestions to the human self, and influence human consciousness. They used to tie knots in threads and blow upon them, as is the habit of sorcerers.

Magic cannot change the reality and essence of things, nor can it create a new reality. However, a imaginary state comes over the perception and consciousness in the manner that the sorcerer desires. As the Qur'an portrays in the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in Surah Taha (65–69):

"Qalu ya Musa ... al-sahiru haythu ata" (20:65–69): "The sorcerers said: O Musa, will you throw first, or shall we be the first to throw? Musa said: No, you throw first. Suddenly their ropes and staffs seemed to Musa, because of the power of their sorcery, to be running, and Musa became frightened in his heart. We said: Do not fear, you will surely prevail. Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick, and a sorcerer never succeeds, however he may come."

Their ropes and staffs did not really turn into snakes. Rather, Musa (peace be upon him) and the people thought that these ropes and staffs were snakes. To the point that Musa (peace be upon him) became frightened within himself, and it became necessary for Allah to give him reassurance. But the realities became manifest when the staff of Musa actually became a serpent and swallowed up their ropes and staffs.

This is the reality of magic, and we should accept it as such. In this way magic affects people and, according to the sorcerers' signals, influences the senses of people. It creates fear in human psychology and consciousness and causes people pain, and human senses turn in the direction the sorcerer wishes. Enough has been said here to describe the reality of sorcery and the meaning of blowing on knots. This is an evil from which we are commanded to seek refuge with Allah and to place ourselves under Allah's protection.

Some narrations state, some of which are not mutawatir though they are sahih, that Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew, cast a spell upon the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. Some narrations say its effect lasted a few days, and others say it lasted several months, so much so that he would imagine he had gone to his wives when he had not gone, and sometimes would feel that he had done a thing when he had not done it, as some narrations report. Then these surahs were revealed for the purpose of exorcism, and when that magical object was brought and these surahs were recited over it, the knots were untied and the evil effect ended, as some narrations report.

But these narrations are contrary to the fundamental belief in the infallibility of the prophets, that they are free from error in all their actions and in conveying the message. Our belief is that the sayings and actions of the Prophet ﷺ are Sunnah and Shariah. These narrations also conflict with this. Furthermore, the Qur'an has explicitly refuted the accusation that he had been bewitched, since the polytheists would claim that someone had bewitched him, which is why he says such things. Therefore, in our view these narrations are dubious. Moreover, beliefs cannot be established by a solitary report (khabar wahid). The source of belief is the Qur'an, and beliefs are established from hadith only when they reach the level of tawatur, and the narrations to which we have pointed are not mutawatir. Moreover, the preferred view is that these surahs were revealed in Makkah, which further weakens the basis of these narrations.

"Wa min sharri hasidin idha hasad" (113:5): "And from the evil of the envier when he envies." Envy means that, on seeing Allah's bounty upon His servants, a person harbours an ill feeling and wishes that the blessing of Allah be removed from that servant. Whether or not, after this feeling, the envier strives to remove the blessings from that servant, or stops merely at the mental impression, since after this impression he may possibly take some harmful action against that person.

Some mysteries of this universe, some secrets of the human self, and some mysteries of the human body are such that our knowledge about them is still incomplete. Therefore we should not vehemently deny them. Some mysterious events occur in these fields, and we cannot reach their essence. For example, the process of transmission of thoughts at a distance, when a connection is established between two individuals; reports of such connections come so frequently that a person cannot doubt them, since many experiments have been conducted and are being conducted on them, and we have no reasonable explanation for the information available to us. For example, magnetic hypnotism (mesmerism), which is being repeatedly tested today, yet no one knows its secret. Apart from the transmission of thoughts at a distance and magnetic hypnotism (hypnotism), many functions of the human body and human psychology whose depths man has not yet reached.

If the envier strives and transfers this impression as harm to that person, we cannot deny this transfer of influence merely because our knowledge and our instruments of experiment have not yet understood the manner of that transmission. For our knowledge of the human self is still elementary, and whatever little knowledge we have obtained has come to us merely by chance. Giving it the form of established reality remains yet to be done.

In any case, the envier's evil exists, and one should seek refuge with Allah from it and place oneself within Allah's protection. It is Allah's grace and kindness that He guides His Messenger to seek refuge in Him, and through him the entire ummah that comes after him is guided to seek refuge in Allah, who provides a shelter from every kind of evil.

Imam al-Bukhari, with his chain of narration, reports from Hadrat A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would lie down on his bed at night, he would join his two palms, then blow into them after reciting "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad" ... "Bi Rabbi al-Nas" (114:1). Then he would pass his palms over the whole body as far as possible, beginning with the head and face, and over the front part of the body as much as possible, and he would do this three times. (This hadith has been reported by the compilers of the Sunan.)

It creates fear in human psychology and consciousness and causes people pain, and human senses turn in the direction the sorcerer wishes. Enough has been said here to describe the reality of sorcery and the meaning of blowing on knots. This is an evil from which we are commanded to seek refuge with Allah and to place ourselves under Allah's protection.

Some narrations state, some of which are not mutawatir though they are sahih, that Labid ibn al-A'sam, a Jew, cast a spell upon the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah. Some narrations say its effect lasted a few days, and others say it lasted several months, so much so that he would imagine he had gone to his wives when he had not gone, and sometimes would feel that he had done a thing when he had not done it, as some narrations report. Then these surahs were revealed for the purpose of exorcism, and when that magical object was brought and these surahs were recited over it, the knots were untied and the evil effect ended, as some narrations report.

But these narrations are contrary to the fundamental belief in the infallibility of the prophets, that they are free from error in all their actions and in conveying the message. Our belief is that the sayings and actions of the Prophet ﷺ are Sunnah and Shariah. These narrations also conflict with this. Furthermore, the Qur'an has explicitly refuted the accusation that he had been bewitched, since the polytheists would claim that someone had bewitched him, which is why he says such things. Therefore, in our view these narrations are dubious. Moreover, beliefs cannot be established by a solitary report (khabar wahid). The source of belief is the Qur'an, and beliefs are established from hadith only when they reach the level of tawatur, and the narrations to which we have pointed are not mutawatir. Moreover, the preferred view is that these surahs were revealed in Makkah, which further weakens the basis of these narrations.

"Wa min sharri hasidin idha hasad" (113:5): "And from the evil of the envier when he envies." Envy means that, on seeing Allah's bounty upon His servants, a person harbours an ill feeling and wishes that the blessing of Allah be removed from that servant. Whether or not, after this feeling, the envier strives to remove the blessings from that servant, or stops merely at the mental impression, since after this impression he may possibly take some harmful action against that person.

Some mysteries of this universe, some secrets of the human self, and some mysteries of the human body are such that our knowledge about them is still incomplete. Therefore we should not vehemently deny them. Some mysterious events occur in these fields, and we cannot reach their essence. For example, the process of transmission of thoughts at a distance, when a connection is established between two individuals; reports of such connections come so frequently that a person cannot doubt them, since many experiments have been conducted and are being conducted on them, and we have no reasonable explanation for the information available to us. For example, magnetic hypnotism (mesmerism), which is being repeatedly tested today, yet no one knows its secret. Apart from the transmission of thoughts at a distance and magnetic hypnotism (hypnotism), many functions of the human body and human psychology whose depths man has not yet reached.

If the envier strives and transfers this impression as harm to that person, we cannot deny this transfer of influence merely because our knowledge and our instruments of experiment have not yet understood the manner of that transmission. For our knowledge of the human self is still elementary, and whatever little knowledge we have obtained has come to us merely by chance. Giving it the form of established reality remains yet to be done.

In any case, the envier's evil exists, and one should seek refuge with Allah from it and place oneself within Allah's protection. It is Allah's grace and kindness that He guides His Messenger to seek refuge in Him, and through him the entire ummah that comes after him is guided to seek refuge in Allah, who provides a shelter from every kind of evil.

Imam al-Bukhari, with his chain of narration, reports from Hadrat A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would lie down on his bed at night, he would join his two palms, then blow into them after reciting "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad" ... "Bi Rabbi al-Nas" (114:1). Then he would pass his palms over the whole body as far as possible, beginning with the head and face, and over the front part of the body as much as possible, and he would do this three times. (This hadith has been reported by the compilers of the Sunan.)

The commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 113, verses 1–5:

In this surah, Allah describes the attributes through which refuge is sought from the evil that is mentioned in this surah.

"Qul a'udhu ... al-falaq" (113:1): "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak." Among the meanings of falaq is daybreak, and another meaning is "creation," in the sense that everything from which existence and life burst forth, as stated in Surah al-An'am (95):

"Inna Allaha faliq al-habbi wa'l-nawa... yukhriju al-hayya min al-mayyit wa mukhriju al-mayyit min al-hayy" (6:95): "Indeed, Allah is the cleaver of the grain and the date-stone. He brings the living out of the dead, and is the bringer out of the dead from the living." And in the following verse (6:96):

"Faliq al-isbah ... husbanan" (6:96): "He is the cleaver of the dawn; He has made the night for rest, and the sun and the moon for reckoning."

If falaq is taken to mean daybreak, the meaning is: the Lord of the dawn, who by spreading light protects everything from the evil that is hidden in darkness. And if falaq is taken to mean creation, the meaning is: I seek refuge in the Lord of creation, who grants protection from the evil of His creatures. Thus in both cases the meaning harmonises with the following phrase.

"Min sharri ma khalaq" (113:2): "From the evil of what He has created", that is, from the evil of all creation, absolutely and in general. Some of Allah's creatures, when they come into contact with others, sometimes produce harm through that contact, while in other circumstances the joining and contact of creatures produces good and benefit. Therefore it is taught to seek refuge from the evil of creatures so that only good remains. And Allah, who is the Creator of these creatures, is able to guide them to a path and to make arrangements such that good emerges from them and evil does not appear.

"Wa min sharri ghasiqin idha waqab" (113:3): "And from the evil of the darkness when it overspreads." Ghasiq literally means one who pours forth, and waqab refers to the opening in a mountain from which water flows. Here ghasiq means night, that is, the night and what is found in it, the night when it bursts forth and spreads over the earth. This night is itself frightening, and its fearfulness increases when in it every hidden and unknown danger may arise: for example, a savage beast may attack, a thief may enter, a deceitful enemy may show his hand, a poisonous insect or snake may bite. Then at night thoughts and whisperings attack a person; pains and sorrows are remembered; the pressure of feelings, passions and inclinations is at its height, all satanic forces are unleashed, evil signs come from every direction, and human desire is at its peak at night. In short, every apparent and hidden calamity attacks at night, because darkness has then spread over everything.

"Wa min sharri al-naffathati fi al-uqad" (113:4): "And from the evil of those who blow on knots." Who are those who blow on knots? They are the sorceresses who afflict people by casting spells on the senses, who deceive the nerves, give suggestions to the human self, and influence human consciousness. They used to tie knots in threads and blow upon them, as is the habit of sorcerers.

Magic cannot change the reality and essence of things, nor can it create a new reality. However, a imaginary state comes over the perception and consciousness in the manner that the sorcerer desires. As the Qur'an portrays in the story of Musa (peace be upon him) in Surah Taha (65–69):

"Qalu ya Musa ... al-sahiru haythu ata" (20:65–69): "The sorcerers said: O Musa, will you throw first, or shall we be the first to throw? Musa said: No, you throw first. Suddenly their ropes and staffs seemed to Musa, because of the power of their sorcery, to be running, and Musa became frightened in his heart. We said: Do not fear, you will surely prevail. Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made. What they have made is only a sorcerer's trick, and a sorcerer never succeeds, however he may come."
